newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Europe unsettled by far-right gains in Austria.
newsitem.headline: Europe unsettled by far-right gains in Austria.

text.p: Europeans greeted big far-right gains in Austria's first European elections with disquiet on Monday, sensing a sea change in the Alpine republic's traditionally tranquil political scene.
"The Austrian election result is a shock for all Europeans," said Helmut Hausmann, European policy spokesman for Germany's Free Democrats, part of the ruling coalition.

Joerg Haider's populist Freedom Party achieved its biggest success to date in Sunday's poll, snatching almost 28 percent of the vote, just 60,000 votes behind Chancellor Franz Vranitzky's Social Democrats on 29.1 percent.
Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel's People's Party, Vranitzky's junior coalition partner, gained 29.6 percent.

Under a headline "Racist winds in Austria", Italy's Corriere della Sera wrote: "Haider's victory, obtained on an openly anti-Europe and racist platform, opens very serious questions about Austria's future."
The Il Messagero daily went one step further. "A new spectre is roaming Europe. It is the nationalist right of Joerg Haider, voted by a third of Austrians yesterday."
Haider, a charismatic, perpetually tanned 46-year-old, fought his most successful campaign to date on an anti-Maastricht, anti-immigration platform.
He rejected European economic and monetary union as defined in the Maastricht treaty and called for an immediate renegotiation of Austrian payments to Brussels.
He argued for a halt to immigration until the labour market picks up and linked foreigners to a perceived crime rise.
European press voiced concern at Austria's lurch to the right and warned against rising nationalism on the continent.
Germany's Dresden-based Saechsische Zeitung drew a parallel between Haider's seemingly-unstoppable advance in the polls and the rise to power in Germany of Austrian-born Adolf Hitler.

"It is true that Haider is no Hitler but it is also true that he has the capacity to become one. Hitler only became what he was because of his success. The less resistance Haider encounters, the further he can go," the newspaper wrote.
France's extreme-right National Front of Jean-Marie Le Pen was alone in welcoming the Freedom Party's "breakthrough".

"The Front National and the Freedom Party share a lot of common ground. Both are against Maastricht and the immigration of their governments and both support a Europe of the 'fatherlands'," National Front spokesman Michel Hubault told Austrian news agency APA.
Since taking over the Freedom Party leadership 10 years ago, Haider has turned it from a political grouping with little support into the strongest far right presence in Europe.
French newspapers noted that the ruling Social Democrats were the biggest losers in Sunday's vote and traced the shift to disenchantment over the European Union.

"In making the euro the scapegoat of all of Austria's woes, Haider made the right electoral choice. The polls show that if the referendum for (EU) membership were held now, most Austrians would vote 'No'," wrote the centre-left Liberation.
Austria joined the EU on a wave of euphoria in January, 1995 but since then deep budget cuts and rising unemployment have soured public perception of the bloc.
Germany's Die Welt noted that while European elections would have little direct impact on domestic politics, they served as a lithmus test of public opinion.

"Vranitzky and Schuessel will no doubt press on with their grand coalition as if nothing had happened," the conservative daily wrote. "But after these elections, Haider's shadow weighs heavy on both coalition partners."
